judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (a) gives "full authority" over benefits, then limits it to "pension, retirement, and such other related benefits as the Board may from time to time determine" — a catch-all against enumerated specifics whose reach is left to the Board.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.2's "certain pension and related benefits" and Recital 4's "pension and retirement benefits" state the same limit differently, and 4.1(c)'s employer indemnity sits against Section 5.9's Fund-side indemnity.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short sentences; the power to "amend or otherwise modify the Plan (from time to time) or terminate the Plan (at any time)" is plainly worded.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 10.1 conditions amendment on a unanimous Board vote and three provisos, and Section 10.3 sets out specific termination routes, so 4.2's unqualified "at any time" power is broader than Article 10 allows.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence permissive statement; "may (but need not necessarily)" is redundant but not ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It tracks Sections 4.1(b), 5.4 and 5.5(k) on insurance contracts without tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The lettered conditions are scrambled — clause (c) appears after the operative sentence and clause (b) is truncated — so the triggers for returning a contribution cannot be read in order.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 10.2 forbids any return or diversion of Fund assets to Contributing Employers "except as otherwise provided in Section 10.3," making no allowance for the refunds Section 4.4 authorises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The anti-alienation text is heavily garbled, with clauses interleaved and the final sentence authorising the Board to "terminate or postpone" payments "to the spouse, children and relatives" of the payee, which does not follow from what precedes it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its carve-outs for QDROs and Plan provisions align with Section 12.15 and Section 4.2, so the trouble is internal to the section rather than a conflict with another provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear designation of the Board as recipient of contributions with all right, title and interest.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.15's denial of any interest in Fund property to employees and Section 5.12's custody rules fit comfortably with this provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short directive that defers wholly to the written Plan; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It expressly cross-refers to Section 4.2 and is consistent with Section 7.2(17)-(18).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All reasonable and necessary expenses ... including, but not limited to" seven enumerated categories is a general-versus-specific structure resting on the elastic word "reasonable."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7.2(8) separately assigns approval of the same expenses to the Board and Section 9.4(a) says collection costs are paid from the Fund while 9.4(b) charges them to the delinquent employer.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional insurance-contract authority clause with a clear non-party disclaimer for carriers.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 4.1(b), 4.3 and 5.5(k); no competing provision found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant runs "in its sole and absolute discretion" over twenty-five enumerated powers and closes with (y), a catch-all to "perform all acts (whether or not expressly authorized herein)" — precisely the general-against-specific problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That absolute discretion has to be squared with Section 5.7's prudence and diversification duty and with Section 8.4, which withholds subsections (j) through (y) from Investment Managers by a garbled cross-reference.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (b) — "two or more Trustees (of which there shall be an equal number of Employer Trustees and Union Trustees)" — is definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.10 defines a Committee as one containing "at least one Employer Trustee and one Union Trustee," which permits unequal committees that 5.6(b) forbids; the two cannot both be applied.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The prudent-person and diversification language tracks ERISA section 404 almost verbatim, so its meaning is supplied by settled statutory usage.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is hard to reconcile with Section 5.5's "sole and absolute discretion" free of state-law investment limits, with Section 5.8's conclusive-reliance protection, and with Section 5.9(b)'s exoneration for "any error of judgment."

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "May accept the same as conclusive evidence of the truth and accuracy" with "no duty to make any investigation or inquiry" is a strong but plainly worded protection.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It pulls against Section 5.7's prudence standard and Section 9.9's audit rights, and its opening lacks the "except as provided by ERISA" carve-out that Section 5.9 contains.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (b) exonerates Trustees from "any error of judgment or ... any loss arising out of any act or omission," which on its face swallows every duty the instrument imposes, and (d)'s "except as may otherwise reimbursed by insurance" is missing a word.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The blanket exoneration cannot be harmonised with Section 5.7's standard of care or Section 5.11's fiduciary-breach insurance, and the opening "Except as may otherwise be provided by ERISA" invites argument about how much survives.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definite bonding requirement pegged to ERISA section 412 with a discretionary top-up.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Section 5.3's expense provisions; nothing elsewhere contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "To the extent not precluded by ERISA, the Fund shall purchase and maintain" is a clear mandatory obligation with a statutory limit.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to Section 5.9 and is consistent with it; ERISA section 410(b) supplies the boundary the clause itself acknowledges.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Deposit and signature-authority rules stated with specifics (FDIC/SIPC institutions; two Trustees, one from each side).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits Sections 5.13, 5.15 and 7.2 on delegation; no competing signature rule was found other than Section 12.6's Chairman-alone conclusiveness.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Ministerial powers or duties" is an undefined line that the section itself does not draw, and the boundary between ministerial and fiduciary acts is exactly what parties fight about.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 5.6(a) allows delegation of "fiduciary responsibilities" to Committees and Section 5.5(r) allows delegation of operational duties, so 5.13's narrower limit does not describe the instrument's actual practice.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Complete authority, in its sole and absolute discretion, to construe the terms of the Plan or this Agreement," with all decisions "final and binding upon all parties affected thereby," is the kind of reservation whose scope is routinely contested.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its finality is qualified by the opening "Except as may otherwise be provided herein," and it must be read against Section 6.6's deadlock arbitration and Section 9.10's mandatory withdrawal-liability arbitration, which take construction questions away from the Board.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A workable execution provision naming the Chairman and Secretary and allowing resolution-based delegation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.6 makes any instrument executed by the Chairman alone conclusive in favour of third parties, which does not match 5.15's two-signature default.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Officer terms "commence on the date of their election" though no election procedure is prescribed anywhere, and "continues" is a grammatical slip.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sections 6.3 and 6.4 govern voting and quorum but never provide for electing officers, leaving 6.1's mechanism unsupported by the rest of Article 6.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (b) lets "any four Trustees" call a special meeting, an oddly high threshold stated without regard to how many Trustees exist.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.1 provides for only five Trustees and Amendment No. 4 reduces the Board to four, so "any four Trustees" becomes all or nearly all of them, making the special-meeting right largely illusory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence quorum rule with a fixed number from each side; nothing ambiguous in the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: With only two Employer Trustees under Section 3.1 (and two Union Trustees after Amendment No. 4), the quorum requires the entire Board, which interacts oddly with Section 6.4(d)'s "lack of a quorum at two consecutive meetings" trigger.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Unit voting with unanimity between the two units is stated clearly, and (d) defines deadlock by example ("including a motion to table").
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It routes deadlocks to Section 6.6 arbitration, consistent with that section, though Section 5.14's "final and binding" Board discretion assumes decisions the unanimity rule may never produce.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and definite: keep minutes, they need not be verbatim, circulate copies.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere in Article 6 or Article 11 competes with it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (a) breaks off mid-sentence at "petition the United States District Court for the Southern" and the deadlock trigger relies on the same "lack of a unanimous vote" formula used in 6.4.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This arbitration route for Board deadlocks sits alongside Section 9.10's separate withdrawal-liability arbitration and Section 5.14's finality clause, three different decision-making channels that must be kept apart.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The opening sentence is broken — "Where the Administrator is a Trust Fund, subject to the terms of this Agreement" has no predicate — and the section is misnumbered "9.2," so the Administrator's responsibilities are introduced by a sentence that says nothing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.1 defines the Administrator as possibly being the Board itself, while this section presupposes a separate person, and item (c) gives the Administrator benefit-eligibility determinations that Section 7.2(15) assigns to the Board.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An eighteen-item list introduced by "without limitation" and closing with item (18)'s general "those functions ... which the Board deems necessary and appropriate" — general catch-all against enumerated specifics, with several items badly garbled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Items (1) and (2) claim a right to "amend, modify or terminate this Agreement at any time," which is broader than Section 10.1's unanimity requirement and provisos and than Section 10.2's flat prohibition on diversion.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three clear subsections on appointing, segregating and self-directing; the only slip is "the Securities of other property."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is echoed almost word for word by Section 8.4(b), which is redundancy rather than conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite mechanics: a Board certificate, an effective date, a written agreement and mutually agreed compensation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to Section 8.8's guidelines and matches Section 7.2(12)-(14); no inconsistency found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, permissive ("may require"), with two precise ERISA references.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.18 defines an Investment Manager as one who "has acknowledged in writing to the Board" its fiduciary status, making the acknowledgment a definitional precondition that 8.3 treats as optional.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The carve-out — powers of Section 5.5 "except subsections (3) through (y)" — misidentifies the starting subsection (there is no (3) in 5.5), so the scope of what the Investment Manager may not do is unreadable as written.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 5.5's lettered list runs (a) through (y) and Section 8.4(b) mirrors 8.1(c), so the defective cross-reference is the only thing that fixes the boundary between Board and Manager authority.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in this Agreement" plus a full liability disclaimer, qualified only by assets over which the Board "has specifically assumed investment management duties."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7.2(13) obliges the Board to monitor and evaluate Investment Managers and Section 5.7 imposes prudence, so a blanket "notwithstanding" disclaimer is in tension with duties the instrument elsewhere imposes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short authority-to-trade provision expressly made "subject to the terms of the investment management agreement."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 8.4 and 8.8; the subordination to the management agreement resolves any overlap.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Shall be the sole responsibility of the Board" is ambiguous between responsibility for setting the terms and legal responsibility for the Manager's conduct.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read the second way it collides head-on with Section 8.5, which says the Board is not "responsible or liable for any acts or omissions of any Investment Manager."

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Wholly permissive ("may (but need not)") with an express anti-inference sentence; clearly drafted.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reinforces Sections 8.5 and 8.2(c) rather than contradicting them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The closing sentence — "Nothing in this Trust Agreement shall be deemed to change, alter or amend any of the terms or provisions of any such agreement" — is a broad subordination whose reach is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is difficult to reconcile with Section 2.5, which deems Employers bound unconditionally to the Trust and all amendments, and with Sections 9.4-9.7, which impose interest and liquidated damages that no CBA need contain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two clauses tying effectiveness and duration of contributions to the CBA; plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches Sections 9.1 and 1.8, and the CBA-driven duration is consistent with Section 1.13's definition of Employer.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A payee-and-form provision; "in the manner and form prescribed by the Board" is delegation, not ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 9.9 supplies the remittance-report mechanics it contemplates; no conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subsection (a) says collection costs "shall be paid from the Fund" and then reverses course with "Notwithstanding the preceding sentence," while (b)'s penalty is "the greater of interest on, or twenty percent of, the unpaid contributions" — a comparison of an unspecified interest amount against a percentage.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It assesses interest "at a rate calculated in accordance with Section 9.5," but Section 9.5(b) states a flat 18 percent rate rather than any calculation method, and Amendment No. 2 makes even that rate discretionary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The list of recoverable items is introduced by "including, but not limited to," so the fixed 18 percent rate sits inside an open-ended catch-all of "any expenses incurred in effectuating such payment."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sections 9.4(a) and 9.7(b)-(c) both cross-refer to "the method set forth in Section 9.5" although 9.5(b) supplies only a rate, and Amendment No. 2 replaces this text with a discretionary rate, so which rate governs a given delinquency is genuinely contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It defines "unpaid contributions" by reference to this Agreement, any CBA "or other agreement," and any Board rules — a broad composite label, though the ERISA hook is precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The same defined phrase is then used in Section 9.7 without repeating the definition, so the breadth adopted here carries into the court-award provision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The five lettered items track ERISA section 502(g)(2) closely, ending with (e)'s open "such other legal or equitable relief as the court deems appropriate."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Items (b) and (c) invoke "the method set forth in Section 9.5," which contains a rate rather than a method, and 9.7(c)'s flat 20 percent differs in form from Section 9.4(b)'s "greater of" formulation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional non-waiver clause; the reference to "Article IX" and then "Article 9" in one sentence is a cosmetic inconsistency only.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves the Union's separate enforcement rights alongside Sections 9.5 and 9.6, which is complementary rather than conflicting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All records deemed necessary by such persons" makes the audit's scope depend on the auditor's own judgment, and "may at any time" sets no limitation period.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 11.1(b) opens the Fund's own books to each Contributing Employer, and Section 9.4 governs the consequences of what an audit reveals; the two fit together without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause forbids litigation of withdrawal-liability claims and then closes by preserving the Fund's right to sue when a claimant fails to arbitrate in time, so "shall not become the subject of litigation in the courts" is only partly true on the section's own terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It also directs New York law "to the extent not superceded by ERISA," overlapping Section 12.2, and stands apart from Section 6.6's arbitration and Section 5.14's finality clause, leaving the boundaries between the three regimes to be worked out.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "At any time and in any manner" is then hedged by three provisos, including (a)'s "not inconsistent with the purposes for which the Fund was established," a standard with no fixed content.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7.2(1)-(2) states the amendment right without any of these provisos, Section 4.2 lets the Board amend the Plan at will, and Section 10.2 imposes a further prohibition, so three provisions describe the same power differently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear prohibition on diverting the Fund, subject to a single stated exception.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exception is limited to Section 10.3, yet Section 4.4 expressly authorises returning mistaken or non-deductible contributions to Employers — a return that 10.2 on its face forbids.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three termination routes are enumerated and (b)'s wind-up direction is definite, though "any remaining surplus in a manner consistent, in their opinion, with this Agreement" leaves the distribution to Trustee opinion.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsection (b)'s "[u]nder no circumstances shall any portion of the corpus or income ... revert or accrue to the benefit of any Employer" is hard to square with Section 4.4's employer refunds, which Section 10.2 routes through this very section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Its records shall constitute the official records of the Plan and Trust Fund for all purposes" is a strong evidentiary rule, but it is plainly worded.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The opening "[u]nless otherwise delegated" defers to Sections 5.13, 7.1(g) and 8.x, and Section 11.2 supplies the valuation rule 11.1(c) presupposes.
